query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of yttrium (Y) to refractory high-entropy alloys can improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a thin, stable yttrium oxide layer at the alloy surface, which acts as a barrier to further oxidation and reduces the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or wrought state
generation.intervention: Addition of 0.1-1.0 at.% yttrium to the alloy composition
generation.conditions: Temperature: 1000-1200°C, Atmosphere: air or oxygen-rich environment, Exposure conditions: static or cyclic oxidation for 100-1000 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, stable yttrium oxide layer at the alloy surface
generation.mechanism: The added yttrium reacts with oxygen to form a dense, adherent Y2O3 layer, which acts as a barrier to further oxidation and reduces the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: A 50-90% reduction in oxidation rate and a significant improvement in scale adhesion, relative to the untreated alloy
generation.boundary: Alloy compositions with more than 2 at.% yttrium may exhibit reduced benefits due to excessive oxide formation
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of yttrium addition and the exact temperature range for maximum benefit may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and exposure conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the oxidation behavior of yttrium-modified and unmodified refractory high-entropy alloys under identical conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-modified alloy exhibits an oxidation rate within 10% of the unmodified alloy after 500 hours at 1100°C in air, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a new class of alloys that consist of more than four alloying elements in close to equiatomic concentrations (). The diverse compositional possibilities of HEAs, combined with appropriate heat treatment conditions, offer the potential to develop new alloys with a combination of remarkable properties such as outstanding mechanical properties, high-hydrogen absorption capacity, and robust resistance to corrosion and radiation (). The refractory HEAs (RHEAs) based on refractory elements were proposed by Senkov et al. () as a new class of high-temperature structural alloys that might surpass the capabilities of nickel-based superalloys. RHEAs are emerging as prominent contenders in diverse industries, notably in the nuclear and aerospace sectors (, ).

The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ).
